prompt: You're building a multiplayer game that sends each player's position 30 times a second. Why do many such games use UDP rather than TCP for position updates?

options.text: UDP encrypts packets automatically
options.explanation: UDP has no encryption at all. Encryption comes from a layer on top (DTLS, QUIC or the game's own scheme).

options.text: UDP guarantees delivery faster than TCP
options.explanation: UDP guarantees nothing about delivery. It's attractive precisely because it doesn't try to deliver everything.

options.text: TCP can't send more than one message per second
options.explanation: TCP can carry very high message rates. The issue isn't throughput but head-of-line blocking and retransmission delay.

options.text: A lost update is superseded 33 ms later, so retransmitting it (and blocking newer updates behind it, as TCP would) only adds lag
options.explanation: Correct. TCP's in-order delivery would hold back fresh positions until a stale one is retransmitted. UDP lets the game drop the stale packet and use the newest state.

workedExample:
1. Updates every 1000 / 30 ≈ **33 ms**.
2. With TCP, if one packet is lost, retransmission takes at least 1 RTT (say 60 ms). Meanwhile the next two updates have arrived but TCP **can't deliver them** until the lost one is filled in.
3. Result: a 60+ ms stutter, all to deliver a position that's already out of date.
4. With UDP, the game just uses the newest packet it has. Important events (a kill, a purchase) can be sent with the game's own lightweight acknowledgements.

prompt: In HTTP/1.1, why did browsers open about six TCP connections per origin?

options.text: HTTP/1.1 closes the connection after every request
options.explanation: HTTP/1.1 made connections persistent by default (keep-alive). The limit is concurrency on a connection, not reuse.

options.text: Each connection can carry only one in-flight request/response at a time, so parallelism needs more connections
options.explanation: Correct. Without working pipelining, a connection waits for each response to finish before the next can be sent; multiple connections are the only way to fetch resources concurrently.

options.text: Servers limited each connection to 100 KB
options.explanation: There's no such per-connection size limit in HTTP/1.1. Connections can carry arbitrarily large responses.

options.text: To provide redundancy in case one TCP connection drops
options.explanation: Redundancy isn't the reason. The six connections are for parallel fetching to work around HTTP-level head-of-line blocking.

workedExample:
1. A page needs, say, 60 resources.
2. On one HTTP/1.1 connection, they come back strictly one after another, each costing at least 1 RTT.
3. At 50 ms RTT: 60 × 50 = 3 s minimum.
4. With 6 connections: ~10 rounds × 50 ms ≈ 0.5 s (plus 5 extra handshakes).
5. HTTP/2 instead multiplexes all 60 on one connection: roughly 1–2 RTTs for requests to go out, limited mainly by bandwidth.

prompt: After moving from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2, your site is faster on office broadband but *slower* for users on a congested mobile network with ~2% packet loss. What best explains this?

options.text: All streams share one TCP connection, so each lost packet stalls every stream until it's retransmitted; with HTTP/1.1, a loss stalled only one of six connections
options.explanation: Correct. This is TCP-level head-of-line blocking. HTTP/2 concentrates everything on one connection, so loss has a bigger blast radius, and every loss shrinks the congestion window that all traffic shares, instead of one of six.

options.text: HTTP/2's binary framing is harder for phones to parse
options.explanation: Parsing binary frames is cheap, cheaper than parsing text HTTP/1.1. CPU cost isn't the explanation for loss-related slowdown.

options.text: HPACK compression fails on mobile networks
options.explanation: HPACK works the same on any network. It saves bytes everywhere; it doesn't make loss worse.

options.text: Mobile networks don't support HTTP/2
options.explanation: HTTP/2 runs inside TLS over TCP; the mobile network just sees encrypted TCP traffic and can't tell the difference.

workedExample:
1. HTTP/2 = many streams, **one** TCP connection.
2. TCP delivers bytes in order. If packet 17 is lost, packets 18–40 wait in the kernel even if they belong to other streams.
3. At 2% loss with ~100 packets in flight, a loss happens almost every RTT, so every stream stalls repeatedly.
4. TCP also cuts its congestion window on loss (by half for Reno, about 30% for CUBIC). With one connection, *all* throughput drops; with six, only one connection's share does.
5. HTTP/3 fixes this with per-stream loss recovery in QUIC.

prompt: Which of these are genuine advantages of HTTP/3 (QUIC) over HTTP/2 (TCP + TLS)? Select all that apply.

options.text: A lost packet only blocks the streams whose data it carried
options.explanation: Correct. QUIC tracks ordering per stream, so loss on stream A doesn't hold back streams B and C.

options.text: Connections can survive a client's IP address changing, for example Wi-Fi to 4G
options.explanation: Correct. QUIC identifies connections by connection ID rather than the IP/port 4-tuple, so it can migrate when the network changes.

options.text: Transport and TLS handshakes are combined, so a new connection needs 1 RTT instead of 2
options.explanation: Correct. QUIC integrates TLS 1.3 into its handshake, and resumption can use 0-RTT.

options.text: It needs less CPU than TCP on servers
options.explanation: Generally the opposite: QUIC runs in user space with per-packet encryption, and has historically cost more CPU than kernel TCP, though offloads are narrowing the gap.

options.text: It works on every network, because UDP is never blocked
options.explanation: Some enterprise firewalls block or throttle UDP 443. That's why browsers keep an HTTP/2 fallback.

workedExample:
Check each claim against how QUIC works:

1. **Per-stream ordering** → no transport HOL across streams. (yes)
2. **Connection IDs** → migration across networks. (yes)
3. **Integrated TLS 1.3** → 1 RTT new, 0-RTT resume. (yes)
4. CPU: user-space UDP plus encryption per packet → typically *more* CPU. (no)
5. UDP blocking exists → fallback is needed. (no)

prompt: A service opens a fresh TCP+TLS 1.3 connection for every call to a downstream API 30 ms away, and each response is about 60 KB. The initial congestion window is 10 segments (~14 KB). Roughly how long does each call take on the network, versus about how long on a warm pooled connection whose window has already grown?

options.text: About 30 ms either way, because bandwidth is high
options.explanation: High bandwidth doesn't help the handshakes or slow start; a new connection can't send 60 KB in one RTT because its window starts at ~14 KB.

options.text: About 60 ms fresh versus 30 ms warm
options.explanation: This counts only one handshake RTT plus one data RTT. It misses TLS (another RTT) and the extra RTTs slow start needs for 60 KB.

options.text: About 300 ms fresh, because TLS needs 4 RTTs
options.explanation: TLS 1.3 needs one round trip for a full handshake, not four. That overestimates the setup cost.

options.text: About 150 ms fresh (2 RTT handshakes + ~3 RTT of slow start), versus about 30 ms warm
options.explanation: Correct. TCP + TLS = 60 ms, then 14 + 28 + 56 KB windows means 3 RTTs (90 ms) to deliver 60 KB. A warm connection with a large window does it in ~1 RTT.

workedExample:
Fresh connection:

| Step | RTTs |
|---|---|
| TCP handshake | 1 |
| TLS 1.3 | 1 |
| Data: 14 KB | 1 |
| Data: +28 KB (42) | 1 |
| Data: +56 KB (98 ≥ 60) | 1 |

5 RTT × 30 ms = **150 ms**. (The request itself goes out with the first data round.)

Warm connection: window already large, so 1 RTT = **30 ms**. Connection pooling gives a 5× speed-up here.

link.title: High Performance Browser Networking: Building blocks of TCP

prompt: Your gRPC clients (HTTP/2) talk to 10 server pods behind an L4 (TCP) load balancer. After a scale-up from 10 to 20 pods, the new pods sit idle while the old ones stay hot. Why, and what's the fix?

options.text: gRPC doesn't support more than 10 servers
options.explanation: gRPC has no such limit. The issue is how connections and requests are distributed, not a server count cap.

options.text: The new pods failed their health checks
options.explanation: Possible in general, but the symptom here is a well-known pattern: healthy new pods get no traffic because no new connections are being made.

options.text: The L4 balancer balances TCP connections, and each client multiplexes all its requests over one long-lived HTTP/2 connection made before scale-up. Use L7 (per-request) balancing or client-side balancing, and/or a max connection age.
options.explanation: Correct. An L4 balancer only decides when a connection opens. Existing connections stay pinned to old pods. L7 proxies (Envoy) or client-side balancing spread individual requests; a max connection age forces periodic reconnection.

options.text: HTTP/2 header compression routes requests to the same server
options.explanation: HPACK compresses headers within a connection; it has no role in choosing servers.

workedExample:
1. L4 load balancing = choose a backend **per TCP connection**.
2. HTTP/2 clients open a connection once and send thousands of requests over it for hours.
3. Scale-up adds pods, but no client opens a new connection, so the new pods get nothing.
4. Fixes:
  - **L7 balancing** (Envoy, Linkerd, an ALB with gRPC support): balance each request (stream).
  - **Client-side balancing**: the gRPC client resolves all pod IPs and round-robins.
  - **`MAX_CONNECTION_AGE`** on the server: e.g. close after 5 minutes so clients reconnect and rebalance.

prompt: You enable HTTP/3 on your CDN. Real-user monitoring shows that on a user's *first* visit, almost all requests still use HTTP/2, yet repeat visits use HTTP/3. Why?

options.text: HTTP/3 only works after a TLS session ticket has been cached
options.explanation: Session tickets enable 0-RTT resumption, but a full 1-RTT HTTP/3 handshake works without them. Tickets aren't required for HTTP/3 at all.

options.text: Browsers learn that an origin supports HTTP/3 from an `Alt-Svc` header (or DNS `HTTPS` record) and so typically start with TCP on the first contact
options.explanation: Correct. Without prior knowledge, the browser connects over TCP; the response's `Alt-Svc: h3=":443"` advertises HTTP/3, which is then used for later connections. Publishing an `HTTPS` DNS record can enable HTTP/3 from the start.

options.text: QUIC needs the server to pre-warm a congestion window per client
options.explanation: QUIC uses normal congestion control starting from an initial window, like TCP. There's no per-client pre-warming requirement.

options.text: The CDN deliberately disables HTTP/3 on first visits for security
options.explanation: There's no such security policy. The behaviour comes from how clients discover HTTP/3 support.

workedExample:
1. A URL says `https://`, not which HTTP version to use. TCP+TLS with ALPN is the safe default.
2. The server replies (over HTTP/2) with `Alt-Svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400`.
3. The browser caches that hint for `ma` seconds and tries QUIC next time, racing it against TCP in case UDP is blocked.
4. To get HTTP/3 on the very first connection, publish a DNS `HTTPS` record (RFC 9460) with `alpn=h3`, which the browser can fetch alongside the `A` record.

link.title: RFC 9460: SVCB and HTTPS resource records

prompt: A server on a 1 Gbps link sends a 90 KB response over a brand-new TCP connection. RTT is 100 ms and the initial congestion window is 10 segments (about 14 KB). Ignoring the handshakes, roughly how long does delivering the response take?

options.text: About 1 ms, because 90 KB at 1 Gbps takes under a millisecond
options.explanation: That's the serialisation time if the window were unlimited. Slow start caps how much can be in flight per round trip, so bandwidth isn't the limit on a new connection.

options.text: About 100 ms, one round trip
options.explanation: One round trip delivers only the initial window of about 14 KB, not 90 KB.

options.text: About 300 ms, three round trips of slow start
options.explanation: Correct. The window grows 14 → 28 → 56 KB, so cumulative delivery is 14, 42 and 98 KB after one, two and three round trips. 90 KB needs three: about 300 ms.

options.text: About 900 ms, because each 10 KB needs its own round trip
options.explanation: The window isn't fixed at 10 KB; it roughly doubles each round trip during slow start.

workedExample:
Track the congestion window round by round:

| RTT | Window | Total |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 14 KB | 14 KB |
| 2 | 28 KB | 42 KB |
| 3 | 56 KB | 98 KB |

98 KB ≥ 90 KB after 3 RTTs → **≈ 300 ms**.

The link could clock out 90 KB in about 0.7 ms. On a new connection, latency, not bandwidth, sets the transfer time for small responses, which is why reused connections matter so much.

link.title: High Performance Browser Networking: Building blocks of TCP

prompt: Over an HTTP/3 connection carrying streams A, B and C, one UDP packet containing part of stream B is lost. Packets after it carrying A and C data arrive fine. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The A and C data that arrived can be delivered to the application straight away
options.explanation: Correct. QUIC orders data per stream, so a gap in stream B doesn't hold back other streams.

options.text: Stream B's data after the gap waits until the lost data is retransmitted
options.explanation: Correct. Ordering still applies *within* a stream, so B stalls until the gap is filled.

options.text: The connection's congestion controller treats the loss as a congestion signal, slowing sending for all streams
options.explanation: Correct. Congestion control is per connection in QUIC, so loss still reduces the rate for everything, even though it no longer blocks delivery.

options.text: All three streams stall, just as they would over TCP
options.explanation: That's HTTP/2's problem. Avoiding cross-stream blocking is the main reason QUIC exists.

options.text: The lost data is never resent, because QUIC runs over UDP
options.explanation: QUIC implements its own acknowledgements and retransmission on top of UDP; it's a reliable transport.

workedExample:
Separate the three things loss can affect:

1. **Delivery of other streams:** QUIC keeps a reorder buffer per stream → A and C unaffected.
2. **Delivery of the same stream:** in-order within B → B waits for the retransmission.
3. **Sending rate:** one congestion window per connection → everyone slows a bit.

So HTTP/3 removes *cross-stream* head-of-line blocking, not every effect of loss. And reliability is still there: QUIC detects the loss from its ACKs and resends the missing frames in a new packet.

prompt: Your site moved to HTTP/2 but still serves images from `img1.example.com`, `img2.example.com` and `img3.example.com`, a domain-sharding scheme from the HTTP/1.1 days. Each shard has its own IP and certificate. What's the effect now?

options.text: A big speed-up: three multiplexed connections are three times faster than one
options.explanation: Multiplexing on one connection already removes the reason for sharding. Extra connections add setup cost and compete with each other; they don't triple speed.

options.text: Each shard costs its own DNS lookup, TCP and TLS handshakes and slow start, and splits traffic across separate congestion windows and priority schemes; removing the shards usually helps
options.explanation: Correct. Sharding existed to get around the 6-connection limit. Under HTTP/2 it brings back the handshake cost and defeats the single-connection design.

options.text: No effect, because browsers merge all subdomains into one HTTP/2 connection automatically
options.explanation: Browsers can only *coalesce* connections when the hostnames resolve to the same IP and one certificate covers them all. Separate IPs and certificates rule that out here.

options.text: Images will fail to load, because HTTP/2 forbids multiple hostnames
options.explanation: HTTP/2 has no such rule. Pages load resources from many origins all the time.

workedExample:
1. HTTP/1.1 problem: one request at a time per connection, ~6 connections per origin → shard to get more connections.
2. HTTP/2: unlimited concurrent streams on one connection → that problem is gone.
3. Keeping shards: 3 extra origins × (DNS + TCP + TLS) ≈ 3 extra round trips each, plus 3 fresh slow-start windows.
4. Each connection is also prioritised separately, so the browser can't order images against CSS and scripts globally.
5. Fix: serve from one origin, or make the shards coalescible (same IP, one certificate covering all names).

prompt: You enable HTTP/3 behind an L4 load balancer that hashes each UDP packet's 4-tuple (source and destination IP and port) to pick a backend. Users on phones report that downloads restart whenever they walk out of Wi-Fi range onto mobile data. Why?

options.text: QUIC doesn't support connection migration
options.explanation: It does: connections are identified by a connection ID, so they can survive an address change. The migration is failing at the load balancer, not in the protocol.

options.text: Mobile networks block HTTP/3
options.explanation: If mobile networks blocked UDP, the connection would fall back to HTTP/2, not restart mid-download after a network change.

options.text: The phone's new IP address changes the 4-tuple, so the balancer hashes its packets to a different backend that has no state or keys for the connection
options.explanation: Correct. The client migrated correctly, but the balancer routed by 4-tuple. Route by QUIC connection ID (for example with a QUIC-aware balancer that decodes server-chosen IDs) so packets keep reaching the same backend.

options.text: TLS session tickets expire when the IP changes
options.explanation: Tickets aren't tied to the client's IP. And migration doesn't need a new handshake at all; the existing connection continues.

workedExample:
1. Before: phone on Wi-Fi, 4-tuple `(198.51.100.4:51000 → VIP:443)` → hashes to backend 3.
2. Phone switches to mobile data: new source IP and port → new 4-tuple.
3. QUIC on the phone carries on with the **same connection ID**.
4. The L4 balancer hashes the *new* 4-tuple → backend 7, which has never seen this connection → it can't decrypt and drops or resets.
5. Fix: have backends encode a routing hint in the connection IDs they issue and have the balancer route on it (the IETF QUIC-LB work describes this), or use a QUIC-aware balancer.

prompt: Your site advertises HTTP/3. A customer's corporate network blocks all outbound UDP. What do their employees experience?

options.text: The site is unreachable from that network until HTTP/3 is disabled
options.explanation: Browsers never depend on HTTP/3 alone. Because UDP blocking is common, they always keep a TCP path available.

options.text: The site works over HTTP/2 (or HTTP/1.1) on TCP, perhaps after a short delay the first time QUIC is tried and fails
options.explanation: Correct. Browsers race or fall back from QUIC to TCP, and remember that QUIC failed for a while. Users lose HTTP/3's benefits but nothing breaks.

options.text: The browser tunnels QUIC over TCP port 443
options.explanation: Browsers don't encapsulate QUIC in TCP; they just use HTTP/2 over TCP and TLS instead.

options.text: Requests succeed over UDP port 53 instead
options.explanation: Browsers don't move web traffic to the DNS port. UDP 53 is for DNS queries to resolvers.

workedExample:
1. Discovery via `Alt-Svc` or an `HTTPS` DNS record tells the browser HTTP/3 is *available*, not mandatory.
2. The browser attempts QUIC on UDP 443; the packets are dropped.
3. It has a TCP connection racing alongside (or starts one after a short timeout) and uses HTTP/2 over it.
4. It marks QUIC as broken for that network for a while, so later loads go straight to TCP.

This is why every HTTP/3 deployment still needs a healthy HTTP/2 path.
